screens.title: Introduction to Ansible for System Automation
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will meet Ansible as a practical automation engine and learn why it is a common choice for system automation. We will focus on what makes Ansible simple: it is agentless, uses declarative descriptions, and relies on standard remote protocols. You will learn the roles of the control node and managed nodes, how to install Ansible on a Red Hat Enterprise Linux system using the system package manager, and how to define a small inventory to list hosts. We also demonstrate ad-hoc commands you can use for quick checks during troubleshooting. By the end of the chapter you will be able to install Ansible, verify the installation, create a basic inventory file, and run an ad-hoc ping to confirm connectivity. A concrete example will walk you through creating a one-file inventory and using a connectivity check to produce a pong response. Watch for common pitfalls such as incorrect hostnames, wrong SSH user settings, or missing private key paths — these are the usual causes when an ad-hoc command fails. Consider how idempotency and the declarative approach reduce accidental changes when you repeat tasks.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Introduction to Ansible
Introduction to Ansible for System Automation
Agentless automation, inventories, installation, and ad-hoc commands.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
What you will understand

This chapter explains Ansible's design goals: simplicity, agentless operation, and declarative automation. You will see how a control node manages many hosts via an inventory and why ad-hoc commands let you test connectivity quickly without writing a playbook.

In this lesson
Install Ansible on RHEL, create a basic inventory, and run ad-hoc commands to verify connectivity.
Why it matters
Agentless automation reduces maintenance and speeds team onboarding when managing servers at scale.

Managed Nodes
Servers reached over SSH or WinRM
Explore key topics
Agentless
No agents; uses standard protocols.
Inventory
List and group hosts for targeting.
Ad-hoc
Run one-off checks and commands quickly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why Ansible’s agentless design is useful, describe the roles of control and managed nodes, install and verify Ansible on a Red Hat Enterprise Linux system, and create a simple inventory to target hosts. Each objective links a specific skill to practical outcomes: you will justify how agentless communication reduces operational overhead, identify the control node as the central point of automation, and configure a basic inventory file to group hosts logically. Installing Ansible and checking the software version teaches you to confirm your environment before running automation. Finally, you will execute and interpret ad-hoc commands to check connectivity and run quick tasks. These objectives matter because they move you from conceptual understanding to hands-on competence: you’ll be able to set up a working control node, verify connectivity with a managed node, and troubleshoot the most common mistakes such as wrong hostnames or SSH key paths. Consider how these skills form the foundation for writing playbooks later — inventory and connectivity checks save time and reduce errors when you scale automation.

screens.title: How these skills connect
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives are tightly connected: knowing Ansible’s agentless design reduces configuration tasks when you set up a control node; understanding control versus managed nodes clarifies where you run commands and where changes land; installing and verifying Ansible ensures your automation engine is healthy; and a correct inventory lets you reach the intended hosts. For example, if you install Ansible but use the wrong SSH user in the inventory, connectivity checks will fail — so inventory and installation skills are practiced together. You will see a hands-on activity that asks you to install Ansible on a RHEL control node, create a one-file inventory, and run two ad-hoc commands: a connectivity check and a simple system command to inspect uptime or hostname. Learning to interpret the module output — success, changed, or failed — is crucial for diagnosing misconfiguration. Keep an eye out for common misconceptions: agentless does not mean insecure, it means fewer moving parts but still requires correct SSH keys and access policies. Practicing these steps once makes later playbook development smoother and more reliable.

screens.title: Agentless Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible’s agentless architecture means you do not install and run a special background process on every managed server. Instead, the control node connects to the managed node using standard remote protocols. On Linux and UNIX systems this is typically SSH; for Windows there are Windows remote management protocols. The practical effect is reduced operational overhead: there is nothing extra to update or secure on each host beyond the usual remote access controls. A concrete example: if you have ten web servers, you only maintain Ansible on the control node and your SSH keys or accounts on the hosts, instead of managing ten separate agents. That reduces configuration drift and simplifies upgrades. A common misconception is to assume agentless means no authentication; it does not. You still need valid SSH credentials and appropriate privilege escalation settings when a task requires root. Also agentless does not eliminate network or permission issues. Typical troubleshooting steps include testing SSH access from the control node to the host with the same user and key you plan to use in your inventory. The takeaway is simple: agentless lowers the number of moving parts while relying on secure, well-understood OS-native remote access.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Agentless Architecture
Definition
Agentless: no special software runs on the managed node
  • Uses SSH or platform-native protocols to run tasks.
  • Only the control node needs Ansible installed.
  • Reduces per-host maintenance and upgrade burden.
Analogy
Think of the control node as a remote operator who logs into workstations using existing secure access rather than shipping a new helper app to every workstation.
Example and common pitfall
Example: ten servers need the same package installed. With agentless Ansible you configure the control node and ensure SSH keys are in place on each server. Pitfall: using the wrong SSH user or key in your inventory causes connection failures even though Ansible itself is installed correctly.
Common mistake
Assuming agentless removes the need for credentials. Always verify SSH access with the same account and key configured in Ansible.
Key Takeaway

Agentless reduces maintenance but requires correct remote access credentials and network connectivity to each managed node.

screens.title: Control Node and Managed Nodes
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible’s operational model uses two primary roles: the control node and managed nodes. The control node is the single machine where Ansible is installed and from which you run automation tasks. It holds configuration files, your inventory, and any playbooks or modules you use. Managed nodes are the remote systems you control: they can be physical servers, virtual machines, cloud instances, or network devices. Communication for Linux and UNIX managed nodes happens over SSH; for Windows targets a different remote mechanism is used. A concrete scenario: on your laptop or a dedicated server you install Ansible and prepare an inventory listing three web hosts and two database hosts. When you run an ad-hoc ping or a playbook, the control node opens secure remote connections to each managed node, executes the module or command there, and collects results. Common misconceptions include thinking managed nodes need Ansible installed — they do not — or that the control node must be powerful; in many small setups a developer workstation suffices. The key operational responsibility is ensuring the control node has network reachability, correct credentials, and access to the inventory that defines the targets.

keyIdea.title: Two-role model
keyIdea.text: Control node runs Ansible and initiates actions; managed nodes are targets reached over standard protocols; no agent required on targets.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Control & Managed Nodes
Roles
Control node vs Managed node
  • Control node: runs Ansible, stores inventory and playbooks.
  • Managed nodes: targets where modules execute over SSH or platform-specific protocols.
  • Control node gathers output and reports status back to the operator.
Concrete example
Imagine a control node with an inventory listing three web servers and two database servers. When you request a package update, the control node opens SSH to each managed node, runs the package module there, and collects success or failure results. You do not install Ansible on those managed nodes.
Pro tip
Keep the inventory and any key files for the control node under version control so team members reproduce the environment.
Key Takeaway

The control node orchestrates actions and should have network connectivity and credentials to managed nodes; managed nodes need only standard remote access configured.

screens.title: Installing Ansible on RHEL
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Ansible on Red Hat Enterprise Linux is a focused process that starts with ensuring your system subscription and repositories are available. The recommended method on RHEL 8 and 9 is to install from AppStream using the distribution package manager. In practice you will run the package installation with elevated privileges and then confirm the binary and environment. Verifying the installation shows the Ansible version, the Python runtime it uses, and important lookup paths for configuration and collections. A concrete example of the verification step is running the Ansible version query on your control node; the output lists the Ansible version and the locations Ansible searches for configuration. Common mistakes include missing repository access or forgetting to run with the required privileges, which leads to package not found errors. Another common oversight is not checking the version after installation — different versions can change default behaviors and plugin paths. The process steps to remember are: ensure repositories and subscription access, install via the package manager, and run the tool’s version query to confirm installation and paths. Installing Ansible on RHEL means ensure repository access, install ansible via the rhel package manager, and verify the runtime and configuration paths by querying the tool’s version output.. In practical terms, prepare the control node and verify the installation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Installing Ansible
Step-by-step
  1. Confirm your RHEL subscription and repository access.
  2. Use the package manager to install the ansible package from AppStream.
  3. Run the Ansible version check to confirm the install and paths.
Verification
The version output confirms executable location, Python runtime, and default configuration search paths.
Terminal demo panel
# Example commands shown for reference in the UI
sudo dnf install ansible -y
ansible --version
Note: Run commands on the control node with appropriate privileges and confirm repository access first.
Key Takeaway

Install via the RHEL package manager and always confirm the installation with a version check before proceeding to inventory configuration.

screens.title: Inventory Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: The inventory is Ansible’s record of which hosts it may manage and how to reach them. By default Ansible looks for a system-wide inventory, but you can provide a local file when you run commands. Inventories can be INI-style or YAML; the simple INI form remains common for small, static environments. An inventory defines groups, hostnames or IP addresses, and optional variables that apply to a group or all hosts. A concrete inventory example lists web servers and database servers with a global section specifying the SSH user and private key path. If the control node cannot reach a host, verify the hostname or IP in the inventory and the correct SSH user and private key. Mistakes here are the usual cause of connection failures. For real environments inventories often move to dynamic sources, but a static INI inventory is ideal for learning and quick labs. The inventory is central because it determines the scope of any ad-hoc command or playbook run, so keeping it accurate and under version control reduces errors as automation scales. Inventory Fundamentals means inventory lists targets and variables; a correct inventory ensures ansible connects to the intended hosts with the right credentials.. In practical terms, how ansible finds and groups hosts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Inventory Fundamentals
What an inventory contains
  • Groups that logically collect hosts.
  • Host identifiers: hostnames or IP addresses.
  • Group or global variables such as SSH user or private key path.
Common formats: INI for static lists, YAML or dynamic scripts for more advanced environments.
Example inventory (INI)
# ~/my_inventory.ini
[webservers]
web1.example.com
web2.example.com

[databases]
db1.example.com
db2.example.com

[all:vars]
ansible_user=devops
ansible_ssh_private_key_file=/home/devops/.ssh/id_rsa
Replace hostnames and paths with your environment values when you test connectivity.
Common mistake
Incorrect hostname, wrong SSH user, or wrong key path are the most frequent causes of failed connections from the control node.
Key Takeaway

Keep inventories accurate and versioned; test each host with a connectivity check before running larger automation jobs.

screens.title: Creating a Basic INI Inventory
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a simple INI-style inventory is a practical first step. Start by placing a file in your home directory and define groups that make sense for your environment, such as webservers and databases. In each group list hostnames or IP addresses. At the bottom you can add group-wide variables under a special header to set the SSH user and the private key path for all hosts. A concrete example is a file with a servers group containing a managed node IP and a global vars section that sets ansible_user and the path to the SSH key. After creating the file, run an ad-hoc connectivity check to validate the entries. A common misconception is that inventory variables must be complex; for most tasks a simple global SSH user and key are sufficient. Another tip: keep the inventory in plain text so you can version control it. If a host cannot be reached, re-check the hostname or IP and the key path; these errors are far more common than issues with Ansible itself. This inventory practice keeps your automation predictable and reproducible.

keyIdea.title: Create and test
keyIdea.text: Author a small INI inventory with groups and global variables, then validate it using an ad-hoc connectivity check to catch hostname or credential errors early.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Creating a Basic INI Inventory
Template
# ~/my_inventory.ini
[servers]
your_managed_node_ip ansible_user=your_ssh_username ansible_ssh_private_key_file=/home/your_ssh_username/.ssh/id_rsa
Replace placeholders with your managed node IP and SSH user. Keep permissions on the key file correct.
Checklist
  • File path is accessible to the control node user.
  • Hostnames or IPs are correct and resolvable.
  • SSH key paths point to readable private keys.
Try this
Create the file in your home directory and run a connectivity check to validate that the control node can reach the managed node using the provided credentials.
Key Takeaway

A minimal INI inventory is an easy, versionable way to declare targets and credentials for your control node to use during ad-hoc checks and later playbook runs.

screens.title: Running Ad-Hoc Commands
screens.narratorSegment: Ad-hoc commands let you run a single module or command across hosts without writing a playbook. The general pattern requires you to target a group or host, specify the module to run, and pass arguments for that module. Typical uses include quick connectivity checks and immediate system queries like uptime or hostname. A common first check is a module that returns a simple confirmation from every reachable host. When you run ad-hoc commands, the output shows whether each host returned success, changed state, or failed, and that output is often enough to diagnose common problems such as authentication or path errors. A frequent mistake is forgetting to supply the correct inventory file when your inventory is not in the default location; always provide the inventory parameter if you store it elsewhere. Another is using a module that expects a shell environment without specifying the proper module; prefer the safer command module for simple commands. Practice by pinging hosts then running a simple command to print the hostname; these steps build confidence before creating playbooks. In practical terms, syntax, examples, and interpreting output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Running Ad-Hoc Commands
Usage pattern
An ad-hoc command requires a target pattern, a module, and arguments. It is ideal for quick tests and single-step operations where a playbook would be unnecessary overhead.
Common checks include connectivity and simple remote queries such as uptime or hostname.
Example commands
# Example shown in the UI:
ansible all -m ping
ansible webservers -m command -a "uptime"
If your inventory is not the default, include -i path-to-inventory when running commands.
Interpreting output
Look for SUCCESS, CHANGED, or FAILED per host and use that to guide debugging.
Pitfall
Forgetting -i when your inventory is custom or expecting elevated results without specifying become in playbooks.
Pro tip
Prefer the command module for simple non-piped commands and the shell module only when you need shell features like pipes or expansion.

screens.title: Declarative Language & Idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible uses a declarative style: you state the desired end state, and Ansible figures out the steps to reach that state. This differs from imperative approaches where you list exact steps in sequence. Declarative automation improves readability and reduces accidental drift because the intent is explicit. Closely linked is the idea of idempotency: a task is idempotent when running it multiple times produces the same result as running it once. For example, if you declare that a package should be present, the package manager will install it if missing; running the same declaration again will not reinstall or alter the system if it already satisfied the condition. A common misconception is equating idempotency with immutability; idempotency means repeated application is safe and predictable, not that nothing can change. The practical consequence: you can safely re-run playbooks on a schedule or during deployment pipelines without worrying about unnecessary changes. For troubleshooting, idempotency helps you identify genuine changes versus no-ops in the automation output. Declarative Language & Idempotency means declare desired state; ansible ensures the state holds and avoids unnecessary changes when the state is already satisfied.. In practical terms, what declarative means and why idempotency matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

For troubleshooting, idempotency helps you identify genuine changes versus no-ops in the automation output. Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Declarative & Idempotent
Declarative vs Imperative
Declarative: describe desired state. Imperative: provide exact steps. Declarative code is easier to reason about across teams.
Idempotency
Applying the same declaration repeatedly does not produce additional side effects once the desired state is reached.
Why it matters
  • Makes automation repeatable and safe for scheduled runs.
  • Helps separate intent from implementation details.
  • Reduces unexpected changes when collaborating across teams.
Misconception
Idempotency does not mean immutability: resources can still change externally; idempotency ensures repeated automation returns to the declared state or does nothing if already satisfied.
Key Takeaway

Declare the state you want and rely on idempotent modules so re-running automation is safe and predictable.

screens.title: Lab Activity: Install and Run Your First Ad-Hoc Command
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through installing Ansible and running a simple ad-hoc command to validate connectivity. First, on your designated control node ensure repository access and then install Ansible using the system package manager with elevated privileges. Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Lab Activity
Activity checklist
  1. Install Ansible using the package manager with elevated privileges.
  2. Run the Ansible version check to confirm installation.
  3. Create ~/my_inventory.ini with a servers group and the managed node entry.
  4. Run a connectivity check using the ping module against the servers group.
  5. Run a simple command module to get hostname or uptime from the managed node.
Inventory example
[servers]
your_managed_node_ip ansible_user=your_ssh_username ansible_ssh_private_key_file=/home/your_ssh_username/.ssh/id_rsa
Ad-hoc examples
ansible servers -i ~/my_inventory.ini -m ping
ansible servers -i ~/my_inventory.ini -m command -a "uptime"
Key Takeaway

Complete the checklist to ensure your control node can reach managed nodes; this foundation prevents common playbook failures later.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Connectivity and Inventory Errors
screens.narratorSegment: When an ad-hoc command fails the usual suspects are inventory errors, SSH credential issues, and network reachability. Start troubleshooting by isolating the failure: confirm the host resolves and is reachable from the control node using standard network tools. Next, verify the SSH user and private key specified in the inventory are correct and that the key file permissions allow the control node to use it. If you see permission denied errors, check the key ownership and file mode. Another frequent issue is omitting the correct inventory file path when your inventory is not in the default location; include the inventory parameter to ensure Ansible reads the intended file. For elevated tasks that require root access, remember ad-hoc commands may need extra configuration for privilege escalation; this is typically handled in playbooks rather than single-line ad-hoc commands. A misconception is blaming Ansible when the issue is simple SSH configuration; methodically validating connectivity, credentials, and inventory entries often resolves most failures quickly. The goal is a repeatable check routine so you can prove the control node can reach and authenticate to each managed node before automation at scale.

Quick diagnostic steps
  1. Ping or reach the host from the control node to confirm network reachability.
  2. Attempt SSH with the same user and key configured in the inventory.
  3. Confirm the inventory file path and group names used in commands.

Common error messages
Permission denied usually indicates SSH key or user mismatch. Name or address not found indicates DNS or inventory typo. Failed tasks with privilege problems may require become configuration in playbooks.
If stuck
Isolate the issue by testing native SSH outside of Ansible, then confirm the same credentials work inside Ansible once fixed.

Systematic checks of network, SSH credentials, and inventory paths fix most connectivity problems quickly and reliably.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will meet Ansible as a practical automation engine and learn why it is a common choice for system automation. We will focus on what makes Ansible simple: it is agentless, uses declarative descriptions, and relies on standard remote protocols. You will learn the roles of the control node and managed nodes, how to install Ansible on a Red Hat Enterprise Linux system using the system package manager, and how to define a small inventory to list hosts. We also demonstrate ad-hoc commands you can use for quick checks during troubleshooting. By the end of the chapter you will be able to install Ansible, verify the installation, create a basic inventory file, and run an ad-hoc ping to confirm connectivity. A concrete example will walk you through creating a one-file inventory and using a connectivity check to produce a pong response. Watch for common pitfalls such as incorrect hostnames, wrong SSH user settings, or missing private key paths — these are the usual causes when an ad-hoc command fails. Consider how idempotency and the declarative approach reduce accidental changes when you repeat tasks.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why Ansible’s agentless design is useful, describe the roles of control and managed nodes, install and verify Ansible on a Red Hat Enterprise Linux system, and create a simple inventory to target hosts. Each objective links a specific skill to practical outcomes: you will justify how agentless communication reduces operational overhead, identify the control node as the central point of automation, and configure a basic inventory file to group hosts logically. Installing Ansible and checking the software version teaches you to confirm your environment before running automation. Finally, you will execute and interpret ad-hoc commands to check connectivity and run quick tasks. These objectives matter because they move you from conceptual understanding to hands-on competence: you’ll be able to set up a working control node, verify connectivity with a managed node, and troubleshoot the most common mistakes such as wrong hostnames or SSH key paths. Consider how these skills form the foundation for writing playbooks later — inventory and connectivity checks save time and reduce errors when you scale automation.

These four objectives are tightly connected: knowing Ansible’s agentless design reduces configuration tasks when you set up a control node; understanding control versus managed nodes clarifies where you run commands and where changes land; installing and verifying Ansible ensures your automation engine is healthy; and a correct inventory lets you reach the intended hosts. For example, if you install Ansible but use the wrong SSH user in the inventory, connectivity checks will fail — so inventory and installation skills are practiced together. You will see a hands-on activity that asks you to install Ansible on a RHEL control node, create a one-file inventory, and run two ad-hoc commands: a connectivity check and a simple system command to inspect uptime or hostname. Learning to interpret the module output — success, changed, or failed — is crucial for diagnosing misconfiguration. Keep an eye out for common misconceptions: agentless does not mean insecure, it means fewer moving parts but still requires correct SSH keys and access policies. Practicing these steps once makes later playbook development smoother and more reliable.

Ansible’s agentless architecture means you do not install and run a special background process on every managed server. Instead, the control node connects to the managed node using standard remote protocols. On Linux and UNIX systems this is typically SSH; for Windows there are Windows remote management protocols. The practical effect is reduced operational overhead: there is nothing extra to update or secure on each host beyond the usual remote access controls. A concrete example: if you have ten web servers, you only maintain Ansible on the control node and your SSH keys or accounts on the hosts, instead of managing ten separate agents. That reduces configuration drift and simplifies upgrades. A common misconception is to assume agentless means no authentication; it does not. You still need valid SSH credentials and appropriate privilege escalation settings when a task requires root. Also agentless does not eliminate network or permission issues. Typical troubleshooting steps include testing SSH access from the control node to the host with the same user and key you plan to use in your inventory. The takeaway is simple: agentless lowers the number of moving parts while relying on secure, well-understood OS-native remote access.

Ansible’s operational model uses two primary roles: the control node and managed nodes. The control node is the single machine where Ansible is installed and from which you run automation tasks. It holds configuration files, your inventory, and any playbooks or modules you use. Managed nodes are the remote systems you control: they can be physical servers, virtual machines, cloud instances, or network devices. Communication for Linux and UNIX managed nodes happens over SSH; for Windows targets a different remote mechanism is used. A concrete scenario: on your laptop or a dedicated server you install Ansible and prepare an inventory listing three web hosts and two database hosts. When you run an ad-hoc ping or a playbook, the control node opens secure remote connections to each managed node, executes the module or command there, and collects results. Common misconceptions include thinking managed nodes need Ansible installed — they do not — or that the control node must be powerful; in many small setups a developer workstation suffices. The key operational responsibility is ensuring the control node has network reachability, correct credentials, and access to the inventory that defines the targets.

Installing Ansible on Red Hat Enterprise Linux is a focused process that starts with ensuring your system subscription and repositories are available. The recommended method on RHEL 8 and 9 is to install from AppStream using the distribution package manager. In practice you will run the package installation with elevated privileges and then confirm the binary and environment. Verifying the installation shows the Ansible version, the Python runtime it uses, and important lookup paths for configuration and collections. A concrete example of the verification step is running the Ansible version query on your control node; the output lists the Ansible version and the locations Ansible searches for configuration. Common mistakes include missing repository access or forgetting to run with the required privileges, which leads to package not found errors. Another common oversight is not checking the version after installation — different versions can change default behaviors and plugin paths. The process steps to remember are: ensure repositories and subscription access, install via the package manager, and run the tool’s version query to confirm installation and paths. In practical terms, prepare the control node and verify the installation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The inventory is Ansible’s record of which hosts it may manage and how to reach them. By default Ansible looks for a system-wide inventory, but you can provide a local file when you run commands. Inventories can be INI-style or YAML; the simple INI form remains common for small, static environments. Agentless means there is no special software running on managed nodes; the control node uses standard remote protocols to reach them.
